rationale: The moments benchmark is a small, loop-heavy numeric C++ program (statistical aggregation over input streams) with no static profile details beyond its Shootout origin, so the weight table favors low-overhead, correctness-safe passes and discounts control-flow passes that tax hot FP loops. SUB gets high weights across the board because instruction substitution is cheap in both size and runtime, semantically safe, and adds meaningful arithmetic-level confusion to numeric code. SPLIT and IGV (which mostly reshapes globals/CFG structure at compile time) are weighted toward high runtime/size favorability and diversity, giving good structural obfuscation nearly for free. IBR and ICALL receive moderate scores: indirect branching and calls complicate static analysis of the dispatch and call graph, which matters for decompilers, but they introduce some indirect-dispatch overhead in tight loops, so their RuntimeCost favorability is mid-range. BCF and FLA are deliberately given low RuntimeCost/SizeCost favorability (and only modest security scores) because bogus control flow inflates loop bodies and flattening imposes a dispatcher on the program's dominant hot loops, where even modest overhead is unacceptable; keeping them in the table at reduced weight lets the compiler apply them only to cold, feature-favoring functions rather than disabling them outright.
